headline: A global AI-driven selloff is deepening: Anthropic's record IPO failed to steady tech, and the S&P 500 is on its longest losing streak since 2020. In healthcare, Sanofi's reported interest in Insmed and new China-competition warnings from a congressional panel lead the news.
watch: Whether the S&P 500 extends its losing streak, and whether Anthropic shares stabilize after the debut
Any confirmation, denial or price detail on Sanofi's reported interest in Insmed
Follow-through on the Commerce Department's AI chip approvals for Chinese buyers, and the fallout for Nvidia and AMD
Treasury yields and gold after the move lower, with the inflation-protection debate still live
Private credit redemption pressure and the ECB's planned scrutiny of bank exposures

paragraphs.text: The biggest healthcare story is a possible large deal. Bloomberg reported Thursday that Sanofi is weighing a takeover of Insmed. Endpoints says that could be one of the larger biopharma acquisitions in several years. Fierce Pharma links it to Sanofi's need to fill the gap left by Dupixent's looming patent expiry, and to Insmed's respiratory drug Brinsupri, which it describes as on track to become a blockbuster. None of the coverage in the list gives a price, a timetable or a confirmation, so this is a report of interest and nothing more. Separately, Sanofi won FDA approval for Infilbray (venglustat), the first US drug for the neurological symptoms of Gaucher disease. BioPharma Dive frames it as a new income source ahead of the Dupixent cliff.

paragraphs.text: Novartis is also working on its patent cliff. Endpoints and Fierce Pharma report that it slightly trimmed the top end of its sales-growth guidance through 2031, tied to upcoming US generic entry for Kisqali, and that it faces a $16.7 billion post-2030 patent hole. CEO Vas Narasimhan told Fierce that most shareholders remain comfortable with the strategy. The company also touted a mid-stage eczema win and said it is working toward restarting trials of its autoimmune CAR-T therapy. Narasimhan, who sits on Anthropic's board, was in London pitching investors on using AI to shorten development timelines.

paragraphs.text: On the regulatory front, Regeneron won FDA approval for Livsayis (cemdisiran), its Alnylam-partnered siRNA drug for generalized myasthenia gravis. It is the second new gMG approval in a week and Regeneron's first marketed RNAi product. It enters a crowded field with AstraZeneca and Argenx. The FDA also criticized J&J for misleading claims about Inlexzo's bladder-sparing benefits, saying the statements rested on uninterpretable data. BMS offered an early, light-on-detail teaser from its phase 3 Alzheimer's psychosis work for Cobenfy. Clinical setbacks piled up elsewhere. Celldex and Bausch + Lomb each reported phase 2 failures, and Celldex dropped the indication. nChroma halved its headcount and scrapped its hepatitis B trial. Evaxion is narrowing to oncology, and Teva's R&D chief resigned a week after the company showcased its innovative-medicines push.

paragraphs.text: Deal and financing flow stayed busy. AbbVie signed a Disco Pharmaceuticals pact worth up to $2.5 billion, with $40 million upfront, for antibody-drug conjugate and T cell engager targets. Arcera agreed to pay potentially more than $1 billion to license Innogen's China-approved GLP-1 for markets outside China. AI-drug-discovery money keeps flowing: Isomorphic Labs added Merck days after a $5 billion raise, and Chinese lab-automation company MegaRobo raised nearly $200 million. Fierce's tracker shows VitriVax at $87 million and Ansa at $71.5 million. Crown Biosciences' planned $204 million sale to China's Adicon fell through. Lilly began construction on its $3.5 billion Pennsylvania plant for obesity drugs including retatrutide.

paragraphs.text: China competition and policy are the other thread. A bipartisan congressional commission warned that China could corner parts of biopharma and flagged licensing deals with Chinese companies. Big drugmakers told a House committee they will halt clinical trials at some Chinese hospitals. That matters for anyone underwriting China in-licensing as a source of cheaper assets. Other items: the FDA is again searching for a leader, per STAT's podcast. Hims and Noom launched peptide programs after HHS eased compounding rules. UnitedHealth sued over lowered Medicare Advantage quality scores, with billions at stake. Healthcare Dive says drug-pricing reform remains stalled despite Republican control of Congress. The Labor Department proposed ending expedited green cards for nurses and physical therapists.

paragraphs.text: The AI trade is unwinding globally. Coverage from Bloomberg, the Guardian, the FT and WSJ describes a worldwide stock slide in which Anthropic's much-anticipated Nasdaq debut did not restore confidence in AI. CNBC says the Nasdaq Composite lost more than 2% Thursday, and MarketWatch notes all 11 S&P 500 sectors fell, with only cybersecurity names bucking the weakness. WSJ says the S&P 500 is heading for its longest losing streak since 2020, and European tech stocks tumbled too. Anthropic's own shares fell after the debut, which several outlets treat as a sign that worries about historic AI capital spending are dominating.

paragraphs.text: Views on what comes next differ. MarketWatch says it is the worst stretch for the S&P 500 since the April 2025 tariff shock, though past six-session losing streaks have often been followed by better returns. Citi strategists, who turned risk-averse more than a month ago, see no compelling reason to add risk yet, and say that if sentiment worsens further, long-duration bonds are the answer. CNBC reports one investor moving defensive as stocks approach key support levels. The FT asks whether defensive stocks are themselves becoming a bubble. These are opinions and historical patterns, not forecasts, but positioning looks cautious.

paragraphs.text: Company news added to the pressure. AMD closed down more than 7% after a short-seller report alleged its firmware appeared at a blacklisted Chinese company, which AMD denies, saying it complies with US law. The NYT reports that lawmakers released confidential information showing the Commerce Department approved sales of more than 800,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, some with military ties. The FT also reports approval of advanced chip sales to Chinese firms. The NYT separately examines Nvidia after Jensen Huang's ouster, noting that its entanglement in US-China relations makes the situation unusual. One bright spot was Apple, which rose in premarket trading on job postings pointing to an agentic AI system.

paragraphs.text: Rates and commodities are sending mixed signals. Treasury yields fell as risk appetite faded. Gold and silver dropped to their lowest levels in more than a year, which WSJ attributes to expectations of tighter monetary policy outweighing safe-haven demand. WSJ opinion argues inflation protection is a no-brainer, and the FT says oil's tight link to bond yields has broken down as inflation pressures spread. WSJ says traders see $85 to $95 oil as the new normal. Oil retreated Friday on better supply conditions despite Middle East shipping risks. Indian refiners are locking in tankers as Persian Gulf disruptions lift freight costs, and Saudi Arabia is helping replenish Japan's depleted crude stocks.

paragraphs.text: Macro data keeps central banks leaning hawkish. US jobless claims rose unexpectedly. Eurozone negotiated wage growth edged up to 2.57% in the third quarter, still modest. Japan's October core inflation was 2.2%, reinforcing expectations of another Bank of Japan hike, and the FT says higher headline inflation as subsidies fade keeps the BoJ on course. South Africa held its repo rate at 7.25%, with the governor saying inflation is well above expectations. China's budget swung to a rare October surplus because of a one-off jump in individual income tax receipts from its offshore-wealth crackdown. In the UK, borrowing rose in October but the fiscal-year deficit is smaller than a year ago, and consumer confidence ticked up. The UK and EU are poised to finalize a relations reset, though the FT says tuition fees remain a sticking point.

paragraphs.text: Private credit coverage today is mostly cautious. Traders Union says borrowers have shown resilience in 2026 while weaker issuers lag. Alternative Credit Investor reports managers are looking beyond rate rises to assess borrower risk. Real Investment Advice argues investors still cannot get out via redemptions. These are commentary pieces with limited detail, but they point to a market where headline performance holds up and the dispersion and liquidity questions are what bite. Hedgeweek asks whether private credit can deliver the alpha that passive emerging-market exposure misses. Supervisors are paying attention: Private Equity Wire says the ECB will scrutinise banks' private credit and hedge fund exposures.

paragraphs.text: One structured-financing item stands out. The FT reports that lenders in a semiconductor financing are trying to bar SpaceX from launching $40 billion of chips into orbit, with investors demanding legal protection for what they see as coveted collateral. Only the headline and sub-headline are available, so the structure and the lenders' names are unknown. It does illustrate how far collateral definitions are being stretched in AI-related lending.

sources.title: Lenders aim to bar SpaceX from launching $40bn of chips into orbit

paragraphs.text: On governance and quality of earnings, the FT reports that Worldline repeatedly withheld payments from suppliers and sought customer advances to bolster cash flow before its results in the years leading up to its 2023 profit warning. Lenders and analysts watch working-capital behavior like this closely. The NYT reports that Delaware's insurance regulator says it was misled about Mark Walter's insurance assets, rejecting criticism of its oversight, and the detail on that dispute is thin. In the primary market, Bloomberg says India's Torrent Power is preparing a rupee bond sale of up to 20 billion rupees ($215 million) as early as next week, its third this year. The WSJ notes Lufthansa is cutting 1,000 jobs at its flagship airline as fuel prices and strike costs weigh on profit, a reminder of the stress high energy costs are putting on cyclical borrowers.

paragraphs.text: The largest announced deal in the list is TPG and Corpay's agreement to buy finance-software platform Bill Holdings for about $6 billion, with TPG taking a majority stake and Corpay a minority interest, per the WSJ. A consortium of Advent and FedEx completed its take-private of Poland's InPost. Diversified Energy closed its $1.8 billion Birch acquisition, which it says lifts Permian production by 35%. Bloomberg reports that an Indian billionaire raised $720 million of private credit to fund the Megha buyout. Private credit is again filling the financing role in a leveraged transaction.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is still the main equity-market storyline. MarketWatch says retail investors turned up, but the offering has not lifted tech more broadly. The FT's post-mortem asks what comes next, and Fast Company looks at how branding may shape its public-company future. The FT reports that shares of some banks and private capital groups that tied their fortunes to AI have fallen this year, so the IPO has not given a boost to the advisers and financiers around the theme. The NYT notes one hedge-fund billionaire made a large gain on Anthropic but sold his OpenAI stake to fund a succession plan, which hints at the secondary-market dynamics around AI stakes. A weak tape could affect the timing of other AI-related listings, though nothing in the list reports a postponement. Energy Connects says a top Japanese power producer is weighing an IPO as AI raises its funding needs.

paragraphs.text: In banking, the WSJ reports that British lender OakNorth, backed by Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and the SoftBank Vision Fund, received a full US banking charter and aims to lend more to growing companies. Banking Dive says Comptroller Jonathan Gould wants to double down on tailored risk and allowing new entrants, which fits with that approval. The FT reports Revolut is facing increased regulatory scrutiny as it grows from a payments upstart into a global bank, and an FT opinion piece argues the US-EU rift on bank regulation is widening and that the ECB needs bolder reforms. Bloomberg says CATL, Luxshare and ASMPT will join the Hang Seng Tech Index in a major expansion, which could drive passive flows into those names.
